prompt: You are merging into a gap in highway traffic. Where should you look as you move in?
choices: Only at the cars behind the gap
Only at your speedometer and mirrors
Check behind, then watch the car ahead
Straight ahead; cars behind must make room
explanation: Check your mirrors and blind spot for traffic behind and beside the gap, then keep watching the vehicle you will follow, since it may slow or stop. Drivers already on the highway have the right-of-way, so they may not make room for you.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. MO p.30, CO p.4)

prompt: Why should you give children riding bicycles even more room than adult riders?
choices: They're small, hard to see and less able to react
They always have the right-of-way over cars
Their bikes have weaker brakes than adult bikes
They are required to ride facing oncoming traffic
explanation: Children are small and easy to miss, they may not judge the speed and distance of cars well, and they can swerve or ride into the street without looking. Slow down and give them extra space.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. MD p.41, MT p.39, CT p.18)

prompt: You see two people walking along the edge of a two-lane road ahead. What should you do?
choices: Keep your speed and tap the horn so they step aside
Speed up so you pass them as quickly as possible
Stay close to the edge so you don't cross the center line
Slow down and pass them with plenty of room
explanation: People walking near the road are hard to see and may move unexpectedly. Slow down and give them as much room as you safely can; if an oncoming vehicle is close, let it pass first so you deal with one hazard at a time.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. KS p.67, UT p.84)

prompt: You are stopped in a line of traffic and see that the car behind you is about to hit you. Besides pressing your head against the head restraint, what should you do?
choices: Grip the wheel and keep pressing the brake
Let go of the wheel so your arms aren't hurt
Release the brake so your car can roll ahead
Shift into neutral to soften the impact
explanation: Keeping your foot on the brake helps stop the crash from pushing you into the car ahead, and a firm grip on the wheel helps you keep control. Bracing against the seat back and head restraint protects your neck.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. CT p.43, NJ p.111, LA p.119, ME p.95)

prompt: A car is passing you on a two-lane road when an oncoming vehicle comes into view. How can you help the passing driver?
choices: Speed up so the driver can fall in behind you
Move toward the center line to discourage the pass
Ease off the gas so the driver can get back in
Brake hard and stop right in your lane
explanation: Never speed up while you are being passed. If an oncoming vehicle appears, slow down and keep right so the passing driver can return to the lane ahead of you; braking hard could cause a rear-end crash.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. OK p.35, TN p.77, MA p.111)

prompt: On a two-lane road, what does a no-passing zone usually tell you about the road ahead?
choices: A passing lane is coming up in a short distance
You may pass there only during daylight hours
The speed limit drops for the next stretch
Your view ahead is too short to pass safely
explanation: No-passing zones are usually marked where hills, curves or other obstructions keep you from seeing far enough ahead to pass safely. Even when a zone ends, pass only if you can see that the way is clear.
ref: MUTCD Sec. 3B.02; state driver handbooks (e.g. CT p.25, TN p.77, AK p.42)

prompt: You are pulling away from the curb into moving traffic. How big a gap do you need?
choices: One just longer than your car
One big enough to get up to the speed of traffic
Any gap, because moving drivers must slow for you
A gap right behind the first car that passes
explanation: When you enter traffic from a stop, you need room to reach the speed of traffic without making other drivers brake. Signal, check your mirrors and blind spot, and wait for a large enough gap.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. CA p.30, NM p.27, MT p.76, KS p.65)
